analysis.one_liner: Gives the FDA power to order food recalls, suspend unsafe food facilities, and require preventive safety plans.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan food safety bill never received a committee vote or any floor action before Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The Safe FEAST Act would have overhauled federal food safety rules. It would let the Food and Drug Administration order companies to recall contaminated food, suspend the registration of facilities that make unsafe food, and require food facilities to identify hazards and put preventive controls in place. It also added rules for imported food, produce safety standards, better tracking of outbreaks, and fees charged to companies whose products fail inspection or need a recall.
analysis.who_benefits: Shoppers and anyone who eats food produced or processed in large facilities. The bill targeted the main gaps in food safety at the time: the FDA could not force a company to recall contaminated food, could not shut down a repeat-offender facility, and inspected facilities on a fixed schedule rather than by risk. People sickened by outbreaks of contaminated produce, peanut products, and imports would have had faster recalls, better disease tracking, and stronger inspection of foreign suppliers.

how_it_helps.text: Gives the FDA mandatory recall authority: companies get a chance to recall voluntarily, but if they refuse, the Secretary can order an immediate stop to distribution and a recall with public notice to consumers [S3].

Allows the FDA to suspend a facility's registration when its food has a reasonable probability of causing serious illness or death, which stops the facility from importing or selling food in interstate commerce [S3].
Requires every food facility to evaluate hazards, implement preventive controls, monitor them, and keep records, with later compliance deadlines for small and very small businesses [S3].

Directs inspection resources by risk so high-risk facilities are inspected yearly and every registered facility at least every four years, and requires an annual public report on how many facilities were and were not inspected [S3].

Requires importers to verify their foreign suppliers meet U.S. safety standards, and sets standards for safely growing, harvesting, and packing fruits and vegetables, with a traceback pilot project to speed up finding the source of outbreaks [S3].
Directs the CDC to strengthen foodborne illness surveillance and share outbreak data more quickly with agencies, industry, and the public [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Food manufacturers, processors, packers, produce growers, and importers, who would face new compliance duties, recordkeeping, reinspection and recall fees, and registration suspension. Some of those costs would likely be passed on in food prices. The bill also contemplates that many state inspections and produce enforcement would run through the Agriculture Department and state agencies, so the federal inspection load is partly shared.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs are real: every facility must write a hazard plan, maintain preventive controls and two years of records, and pay fees for reinspections and recalls, which would fall hardest on paperwork capacity at small firms [S3].

The bill charges industry fees rather than relying solely on taxpayer funding, and those fees only flow if Congress keeps appropriations for FDA food work growing by at least 4.5% a year; if funding flatlines, the fees are refunded and enforcement could be underfunded [S3].

Enforcement of produce safety standards would lean on audit-based verification and state agricultural agencies rather than direct FDA inspection, which critics could reasonably call a lighter-touch approach [S3].
Small and very small businesses get two and three years before the preventive-control rules apply, delaying benefits for consumers in the parts of the supply chain with fewer safety resources [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits would go directly to anyone who buys food: mandatory recalls, power to shut down dangerous facilities, risk-based inspections, and faster outbreak tracing address problems that had repeatedly sickened people through produce and imported food. The costs are compliance burdens and fees on food companies, softened with delayed deadlines for small businesses and state variances for growers. The design is balanced rather than perfect — fee funding tied to appropriations growth is a real weakness — but the core tradeoff is straightforward: safer food at some cost to industry, most of which would likely be passed on in prices.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in two House committees and their subcommittees for the rest of the Congress and never got a markup, a vote, or floor action.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Costa introduced the bill on March 5, 2009 with 22 original cosponsors from both parties, including members of the Agriculture Committee's leadership [S1].
It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Agriculture Committee on the day of introduction [S5].

On March 6 it went to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, and on April 23 to the Agriculture Subcommittee on Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry, with executive comment requested from HHS and USDA [S5].
No further action appears in the record: the bill never received a committee vote or a House floor vote, and the Congress ended January 3, 2011 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food facilities and importers avoided the bill's preventive-control mandates, recordkeeping, and fees, and the FDA gained no new recall or suspension powers from this bill. Consumers got no added protection from this legislation; if the country got a food safety law in this period, it came through a different bill entirely.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Food processors avoided new costs; shoppers got nothing

for.name: Jim Costa
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Safe FEAST Act and recruited a bipartisan group of original cosponsors.

for.name: Collin Peterson
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, an unusual show of support from the chair of one of its two receiving committees.

against.name: Henry Waxman
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the lead committee where the bill was referred; the committee never took it up or reported it to the floor.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on March 5, 2009, sent it to its Health Subcommittee, and took no further recorded action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship split 18 Democrats and 12 Republicans among the 30 cosponsors, with a Democratic committee chair also cosponsoring; the bill never reached a vote, so there was no roll call to divide the parties.

industries.note: The bill would require hazard plans, preventive controls, recordkeeping, and registration renewal, and would let the FDA suspend a facility and order recalls with fees for reinspections and recalls. Consumers gain safer food at these companies' expense.

Importers would have to verify their foreign suppliers meet U.S. standards and pay reinspection and program fees, but a voluntary qualified importer program would offer expedited review to compliant importers. The net effect is higher cost with a fast lane for good actors.

New FDA standards for growing, harvesting, handling, and packing produce, plus traceback recordkeeping, would add costs on the farm. The bill allows state variances for local growing conditions, delays small business compliance, and routes enforcement through USDA and state agriculture agencies, softening the burden.

The bill requires food testing for import decisions and emergencies to be done by federally accredited laboratories, making accredited labs the required channel for that testing. Consumers benefit because test results must go directly to the FDA.
